n: Job begins the final part of his closing speech. Chapter 29 looks back on his happy past; chapter 30 describes his painful present; chapter 31 is his oath of innocence.
Job longs for the months gone by, when he felt God watching over him.
Then God’s lamp shone over his head, and by God’s light he walked safely through dark times.

f.w: his candle shined upon my head

n: Job remembers the prime of his life, when God’s close friendship rested on his home.

f.g: Hebrew sod — God’s intimate friendship or counsel.
Literally “days of my autumn” — his ripe, mature years.

n: God was still with him, and his children were all around him — the loss that hurts most.

f.w: when my children were about me

n: His life overflowed with abundance — as if his paths were bathed in cream and the rocks poured out olive oil.

f.g: Curds or cream — a symbol of richness.

n: Job would go to the city gate and take his seat in the public square — the place where elders gave judgments and settled disputes.

f.g: The city gate was the center of public life and the town court.

n: When young men saw him, they stepped aside out of respect, and old men stood up.
Even leaders stopped talking and covered their mouths to listen to him.

f.w: laid their hand on their mouth

n: Nobles fell silent, their tongues stuck to the roofs of their mouths.

f.w: their tongue cleaved to the roof of their mouth

n: Everyone who heard him praised him, and all who saw him spoke well of him.
Why? Because he rescued the poor who cried for help and the orphans who had no one. This answers Eliphaz’s false charges (22:6-9).

f.w: I delivered the poor that cried

n: People on the brink of ruin blessed him, and he made widows’ hearts sing for joy.

f.w: the widow's heart to sing for joy

n: Job wore righteousness like clothing and justice like a robe and turban.

f.g: A turban or headband of honor.

n: He was eyes for the blind and feet for the lame — a picture of true service.
He was like a father to the poor and investigated the cases of strangers to make sure they got justice.

f.w: the cause which I knew not I searched out
f.g: He looked into the legal cases even of people he didn’t know.

n: He broke the power of the wicked and rescued their victims from their teeth.

f.w: brake the jaws of the wicked

n: Back then Job expected to die peacefully in his own home after a long life.

f.w: I shall die in my nest
f.g: In the security of my home and family.
Possibly “as the phoenix” — the Hebrew word can mean either; both images mean a very long life.

n: He was like a well-watered tree, its roots reaching to water and dew resting on its branches.

f.w: My root was spread out by the waters

n: His honor felt ever fresh, and his strength — pictured as a bow — was constantly renewed.

f.g: The bow symbolizes strength and vigor.

n: People listened to him eagerly and waited in silence for his advice.

f.g: They waited quietly for his wise judgment.

n: After he spoke, no one needed to add anything; his words fell on them gently like drops of rain.
They waited for him like farmers wait for rain, mouths open to drink in the spring showers.

f.g: The spring rains that ripened crops before harvest.

n: When he smiled on them, they could hardly believe it, and the light of his face encouraged them.
He led them like a chief, lived like a king among his troops, and was a comforter to mourners — the very thing his friends failed to be.
